definition: A mathematical curve defined by control points, used to draw the smooth outlines that make up vector artwork. Straight lines are just bezier curves with zero curvature.
Artwork extending past the trim edge so that no white slivers appear after cutting. A 3mm bleed is standard for print production.
The subtractive color model (cyan, magenta, yellow, key/black) used for printing. Unlike RGB, it describes how ink absorbs light rather than how a screen emits it.
Splitting an artwork into individual color layers, each of which becomes a separate screen, plate, or cutting pass in production.
Multiple sub-paths within a single path object, where interior shapes create holes. Essential for lettering and for cutting out shapes from a sheet.
The outline path that a laser, vinyl cutter, or CNC bit follows. Accuracy of the contour determines the quality of the finished cut.
Dots per inch — the resolution of a raster image. Higher DPI means more detail but a larger file; vector graphics have no DPI at all because they are resolution-independent.
Drawing Exchange Format — a CAD interchange format understood by nearly every laser cutter, CNC machine, and cutting plotter. Typically exported as layers or polylines.
Converting artwork into stitch instructions — satin stitches, fill stitches, and run stitches — that an embroidery machine can follow. Stitch density and pull compensation both matter.
Encapsulated PostScript — a classic print-oriented vector format widely accepted by print shops, though it lacks the web-friendly structure of SVG.
The color applied to the inside of a closed path. Paths can have a fill, a stroke, or both.
A smooth transition between two or more colors. Vector gradients scale infinitely and remain sharp at any resolution.
A container that holds multiple objects so they can be moved, scaled, or edited together. Grouping keeps complex files manageable.
The width of material removed by a cutting tool. Because the kerf consumes material, cut shapes come out slightly smaller than the drawn outline.
An anchor point on a path. Nodes define where a curve bends and how sharp a corner is; they are the fundamental editable unit of vector artwork.
Creating a copy of a shape shifted inward or outward by a fixed distance. Used to make cutters, welder gaps, and press-up allowances.
An open or closed sequence of nodes and curves that defines a shape. A single SVG file can contain thousands of paths.
Portable Network Graphics — a lossless raster format supporting transparency. It cannot scale cleanly and is not cuttable by a machine.
A classic open-source bitmap tracer that converts black-and-white images into vector outlines. Effective for line art, less so for color and gradients.
Pixels per inch — the display equivalent of DPI. DPI describes print resolution, PPI describes screen resolution.
Images built from a grid of individual pixels (PNG, JPEG, GIF). They photograph well but blur or pixelate when scaled up.
The additive color model (red, green, blue) used by screens. Adding all three at full intensity produces white.
A printing technique that pushes ink through a mesh stencil, one screen per color. Vector files produce the cleanest separations.
A named premixed ink (Pantone, for example) used consistently across a print run rather than mixed from CMYK. Essential for consistent brand color on physical products.
Scalable Vector Graphics — an XML-based vector format supported by browsers, design tools, laser cutters, and plotters. The native output format for most modern vectorizers.
The outline drawn along the edge of a path, defined by width, color, and cap style. Often used for line art and lettering.
The process of converting a raster image into vector paths by identifying edges, regions, and color boundaries.
Images defined by mathematical paths and shapes rather than pixels. They scale to any size without loss of quality and are the required input for cutting and fabrication.
Converting a raster image into vector artwork. Modern AI vectorizers detect color regions and shapes rather than only edges, producing far cleaner results than simple thresholding.
Removing the unwanted vinyl or transfer film from around a cut design, leaving only the parts you want to keep or transfer.
Combining or subtracting shapes using union, intersection, or difference. Useful for punching holes in letters or merging overlapping shapes.
